overview: This domain covers the daily work of keeping information safe, and what happens when something goes wrong: protecting data through classification, handling, masking, sanitization and encryption; watching systems through logs, triage and threat intelligence; responding to incidents; protecting assets through their lifecycle; and testing defenses. Throughout, the entry-level practitioner follows procedure, protects people first, stays within their role and escalates instead of acting alone.
analogy: Think of a hospital. Patient records are sorted by sensitivity and handled by strict rules (data security). Monitors at every bed feed a central station, where staff decide which alarm needs attention first (security operations). When a patient's condition crashes, a trained team runs a rehearsed procedure in which everyone has a role (incident response). Equipment is tracked, maintained and retired safely (asset protection), and drills and inspections check that it all works (security testing). A new nurse who hears an alarm does not operate alone: they call the response team.

topics.overview: Data is protected by deciding how sensitive it is, then handling it by matching rules until it is safely destroyed. This topic covers classification, handling, masking, sanitization, the cryptography that protects data, and keeping sensitive data out of public AI services.
can_do: Tell classification from labeling, and name who sets a data set's classification
Pick clear, purge or destroy for a device, and explain why deleting files is not sanitization
Match encryption, hashing, signatures and certificates to their jobs, and count the keys each encryption type needs
Explain why pasting sensitive data into a public AI service is a disclosure

subtopics.name: Data Classification and Labeling
subtopics.definition: Data classification sorts information into sensitivity levels, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, so each level gets protection that fits its value.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without classification, secrets get too little protection and public brochures too much. Labels make the level visible, so people and tools apply the right handling rules.
how_it_works: The data owner, the business manager accountable for the data, decides its level.
Levels reflect the harm if the data were disclosed, altered or lost.
A label shows the level to people and systems: a header, watermark, file tag or metadata field.
Data loss prevention (DLP) tools read labels and warn or block when restricted data heads somewhere unsafe.

rows.label: Who does it
cells: Users and systems apply the mark the owner set

rows.label: Output
cells: A visible or machine-readable mark on the data

rows.label: If it is missing
cells: No one knows what protection is needed
People guess, and tools cannot enforce the rules

subtopics.example: A planning officer at a city council saves an unlabeled report on land the council plans to buy in a team-wide folder. Priya, a new security analyst, notices it. Rather than guess a level, Priya asks the report's owner, the planning director, to classify it.

review: Apply the label your policy requires when you create or receive data
Compare folder access with the labels on the files inside
evidence: The classification policy and its defined levels
Labels and access settings on shared folders and files
audit_focus.recommend: Report mislabeled or unlabeled sensitive data to its owner, or to your supervisor if the owner is unknown.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner sets and changes the classification level

subtopics.isaca_rule: The owner decides the level; everyone else applies it. When data is unlabeled or looks mislabeled, ask the owner, and protect it at the higher level until they answer.

exam_traps.trap: The IT team or a security analyst should decide how sensitive a business file is.
exam_traps.why: IT and security protect data but do not own it. The accountable business owner understands the harm of disclosure, so the owner sets the level.

exam_traps.trap: Labeling a file is the same as classifying it.
exam_traps.why: Classification is the decision; the label only records it.

key_terms.definition: The person accountable for a data set, who sets its classification and approves access.
The person or team that looks after data day to day, such as backups, following the owner's rules.

subtopics.memory_aid: Owner decides, label shows, controls follow.

subtopics.name: Data Handling Across the Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: Data handling is the set of rules for how data at each classification level is created, stored, used, shared, archived and destroyed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Data often leaks while it is used or shared, not while stored. Rules for every stage close those gaps and keep the organization within the law.
how_it_works: Handling rules say where data may be stored, who may see it, how it is sent and whether it may be printed.
A retention schedule says how long each type of record is kept, based on legal and business needs.
When retention ends, data is destroyed by a method that fits its level.
A legal hold from legal counsel pauses destruction of records that a lawsuit or investigation may need.
subtopics.example: A logistics firm's rules say confidential customer records must be encrypted on removable media. A sales manager asks Jordan, a help desk technician, to copy a customer list onto an ordinary memory stick for a trade show. Jordan explains the rule, offers an approved encrypted drive and logs the request.

review: Follow the handling rule for the data's label before sharing or copying it
Use only approved storage and transfer methods for sensitive data
evidence: The handling matrix listing rules for each classification level
Legal hold notices listing which records must be kept
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any request to bypass a handling rule with your supervisor, and send legal hold questions to legal counsel.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets handling rules in policy; legal counsel issues and lifts legal holds

subtopics.isaca_rule: Handling rules follow the label at every stage, even after data leaves your system. Keep data only as long as the schedule says, and never destroy records under a legal hold.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping all data forever is the safest choice.
exam_traps.why: Old data can still leak and can be demanded in a lawsuit. Keeping it longer than needed adds risk and can break privacy law.

exam_traps.trap: Records under a legal hold can be deleted once their retention period ends.
exam_traps.why: The hold overrides the schedule. Destroying held records can count as destroying evidence.

key_terms.definition: The stages data passes through: create, store, use, share, archive and destroy.
An instruction from legal counsel to preserve specific records, suspending their normal destruction.

subtopics.name: Data Masking and Tokenization
subtopics.definition: Data masking hides real values behind realistic fakes or partial views; tokenization swaps a sensitive value for a random token that only a secure vault can map back.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Testing, support and analytics often need data but not the real sensitive values. Masking and tokenization let that work go ahead with less real data exposed.
how_it_works: Static masking makes a changed copy, such as a test database with fake names.
Dynamic masking changes only what a viewer sees, such as the last four card digits; the stored record is unchanged.
Tokenization keeps the real value in a protected vault; other systems hold a token with no mathematical link to it.
Only authorized systems can swap a token back, so far fewer systems hold sensitive data.

rows.label: Where the real value is
cells: Not in the masked copy at all

rows.label: Reversible?
cells: The view only; data is unchanged

subtopics.example: A school's software team needs realistic student records to test a new grade portal, and a developer suggests copying the live database. Sam, the junior security analyst on the project, points to the policy banning live personal data in test systems and requests a masked copy from the database administrator.

review: Request masked or synthetic data for testing, never a live production copy
Use tokens or masked views in reports when full values are not needed
evidence: Test environments holding real personal or payment data
Accounts able to reach the token vault and reverse tokens
audit_focus.recommend: Report real sensitive data found in a test or support system to its data owner and your supervisor.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner approves any use of real data outside production

subtopics.isaca_rule: Give each person and system the least real data the task needs: masked data for testing and support, tokens where a reference is enough, and real values in as few places as possible.

exam_traps.trap: Tokenization is just another name for encryption.
exam_traps.why: Anyone with the key can decrypt an encrypted value. A token has no mathematical link to the original; only the vault can map it back.

exam_traps.trap: Masking a name on screen means the database no longer holds it.
exam_traps.why: Dynamic masking changes only the view. The stored value still needs full protection.

key_terms.definition: Changing data so individuals can no longer be identified, even by combining data sets.
Replacing identifiers with substitutes that can be re-linked; the data is still personal data.

subtopics.name: Media Sanitization: Clear, Purge and Destroy
subtopics.definition: Media sanitization makes data on storage media infeasible to recover, by clearing, purging or destroying it, before the media is reused, released or discarded.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Deleting files or formatting a drive removes the pointers, not the data, so free tools can bring it back. Retired laptops, copiers and phones have leaked records this way.
how_it_works: The three methods come from the sanitization guide of NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology.
Overwriting misses spare cells on solid-state drives (SSDs), so they need a built-in purge command or cryptographic erase.
Degaussing works only on magnetic media, so it does nothing to flash storage.
Each sanitization is verified and recorded before the asset record is closed.

rows.label: Stops
cells: Simple recovery through the device's normal interface

rows.label: Typical technique
cells: Built-in sanitize command or cryptographic erase
Disintegrate, incinerate or melt; shred paper

rows.label: Good fit
cells: Reuse inside the organization for lower-sensitivity data
Reuse or resale, including outside the organization
Failed or obsolete media, and all paper

subtopics.example: A hospital is returning 40 leased laptops with solid-state drives. A facilities supervisor asks Alex, an IT support technician, to 'just format them'. Alex explains that formatting leaves patient data recoverable, runs the approved purge tool, and records each serial number and result for the asset manager.

review: Use the sanitization tool and method the procedure lists for the media type
Verify each device and record its serial number and method
evidence: Certificates of sanitization from any disposal or recycling vendor
Asset inventory entries updated as each device is released
audit_focus.recommend: Stop and tell your team lead when a device cannot be sanitized as the procedure requires, such as a failed drive.
audit_focus.decides: Policy and the data owner set the required method for each level

subtopics.isaca_rule: Deleting is not sanitizing. Clear for low-risk internal reuse, purge before sensitive media leaves your control, and destroy when media cannot be purged. Verify, and keep the record.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting the files and emptying the recycle bin sanitizes a laptop.
exam_traps.why: Deletion removes only the file pointers. The data stays on the drive, and free tools can recover it.

exam_traps.trap: Degaussing is the right way to sanitize a solid-state drive.
exam_traps.why: Degaussing uses magnetic force and does nothing to flash storage. Purge with cryptographic erase, or destroy the drive.

key_terms.definition: Destroying the keys to encrypted data, leaving unreadable ciphertext; also called crypto-shredding, and often the only purge option in the cloud.
A record of which media was sanitized, how, by whom and when, and how it was verified.

subtopics.name: Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption
subtopics.definition: Encryption turns readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a key. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; asymmetric encryption uses a public and private key pair.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Encryption keeps stolen or intercepted data confidential, but the wrong type or lost keys leave data exposed or unrecoverable.
how_it_works: Symmetric algorithms, such as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), are fast, so they protect bulk data.
In asymmetric encryption, such as RSA (named after its inventors), the public key is shared; only the owner holds the private key.
To send someone a secret, encrypt it with their public key; only their private key can decrypt it.
Key count: symmetric needs n(n−1)/2 keys, one per pair of people; asymmetric needs 2n, one pair per person.
For 10 people: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45 symmetric keys, against 20 asymmetric keys.
Real systems are hybrid: Transport Layer Security (TLS) uses asymmetric methods to share a session key, then symmetric encryption.

rows.label: Keys
cells: A public key and a matching private key

rows.label: Speed
cells: Fast; suits large volumes of data
Slower; suits small items such as keys and signatures

rows.label: Main challenge
cells: Proving a public key belongs to its owner (see 5.1.6)

rows.label: Typical uses
cells: Disk, database and session encryption, such as AES
Key exchange, signatures and certificates, such as RSA

subtopics.example: An accounting firm partner plans to email a client's encrypted tax file with its password in the same message. Morgan, the IT assistant, explains that an interceptor would get both, and points the partner to the client portal that policy requires.

review: Use approved encryption tools rather than inventing your own scheme
Send passwords or keys through a different channel from the data
evidence: Devices and data stores missing required encryption at rest
Key and certificate expiry dates in the key management service
audit_focus.recommend: Report a lost, exposed or shared private key to the key's owner and the security team immediately.
audit_focus.decides: Security management sets approved algorithms and key lengths in the cryptography standard

subtopics.isaca_rule: Use symmetric encryption for bulk data and asymmetric to exchange keys and prove identity. Encrypt to someone with their public key, and keep keys apart from the data.

exam_traps.trap: To send a confidential message, encrypt it with your own private key.
exam_traps.why: Your public key, which anyone can have, opens it. For confidentiality, use the recipient's public key.

exam_traps.trap: Asymmetric encryption is stronger, so use it for bulk data.
exam_traps.why: It is far slower. Systems use it to exchange a symmetric key, then encrypt the data symmetrically.

key_terms.definition: Creating, storing, rotating and destroying keys under control; strong encryption fails if keys are exposed.
A tamper-resistant device that creates and uses keys without exposing them.

subtopics.memory_aid: Symmetric: one shared key per pair. Asymmetric: one key pair per person.

subtopics.name: Hashing, Digital Signatures and Certificates
subtopics.definition: A hash turns any input into a fixed-length, one-way digest; a digital signature applies the signer's private key to a hash to prove origin and integrity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Hashing shows whether data changed. Signatures and certificates prove who sent data or runs a website.
how_it_works: Changing one character of the input changes the whole digest (see 1.1.3 for integrity versus authenticity).
A plain hash uses no key and cannot be undone, so it gives integrity, not confidentiality.
A keyed hash (hash-based message authentication code, HMAC) adds a secret key, so it also shows the sender held that key.
To sign, software hashes the message and applies the sender's private key; anyone can check it with the public key.
A digital certificate binds a public key to its owner; a certificate authority (CA) verifies the owner, then signs the certificate.

rows.label: Uses a key?
cells: No, for a plain hash; a keyed hash (HMAC) adds one

rows.label: Reversible?
cells: Checked with the public key, not reversed

rows.label: Provides
cells: Integrity; an HMAC also shows the sender held the key
Integrity, proof of origin and non-repudiation

rows.label: Example use
cells: Protecting a file or a session
Signing software, a contract or a certificate

subtopics.example: Staff at an architecture firm see a browser warning on the timesheet site: its certificate is not from a trusted authority. A manager says to click 'continue anyway'. Casey, the IT support technician, asks staff to stop and raises a ticket with the security team, since traffic may be intercepted.

review: Install only software and updates whose signature verifies
Treat certificate warnings as possible interception, never as a click-through
evidence: Signature verification results on updates and scripts
Certificate details: issuer, owner name and expiry date
audit_focus.recommend: Report a failed signature, a hash mismatch or an untrusted certificate to the security team before going further.
audit_focus.decides: Security management sets approved algorithms and trusted certificate authorities in the cryptography standard

subtopics.isaca_rule: A hash shows whether data changed only when the expected value comes from a trusted source, and it hides nothing. A signature proves who sent something and that it is unchanged, but does not keep it secret. When data must also be confidential, encrypt it as well.

exam_traps.trap: Hashing a customer file keeps it confidential.
exam_traps.why: A hash is not encryption; the file stays readable.

exam_traps.trap: A digitally signed email is also encrypted.
exam_traps.why: A signature proves origin and integrity, but anyone can still read the message.

key_terms.definition: Passwords stored with a random value added before slow hashing, so identical passwords give different results.
Proof that a specific party sent or approved something, so they cannot credibly deny it.

subtopics.name: Quantum-Resistant Cryptography
subtopics.definition: Quantum-resistant, or post-quantum, cryptography uses new public-key algorithms designed to stay secure against a future quantum computer that could break today's methods.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers can record encrypted traffic now and decrypt it once a capable quantum computer exists. Data that must stay secret for years is already at risk.
how_it_works: A large quantum computer could break RSA (named after its inventors) and elliptic curve methods, which protect today's key exchange and signatures.
Symmetric encryption, such as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), and modern hashes are far less affected; longer keys keep them strong.
In 2024 NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, published its first post-quantum standards.
Migration starts with a cryptographic inventory: where each algorithm is used, what it protects and for how long.

rows.label: Quantum risk
cells: Low: longer keys keep it strong

rows.label: What to do
cells: Move to the new post-quantum standards
Use long keys, such as AES-256

subtopics.example: A city council's security manager asks Riley, a new analyst, to help prepare for quantum risk. Riley starts a cryptographic inventory: for each system, which algorithms it uses, who owns it, and whether its software can switch algorithms without a redesign. Systems that cannot change are flagged to their owners.

review: Record algorithms and key lengths whenever you document a system
Flag systems protecting long-lived data that rely on RSA or elliptic curves
evidence: The migration priority list and the owner's sign-off on it
Vendor roadmaps for post-quantum support in key products
audit_focus.recommend: Raise systems that cannot change algorithms, such as embedded devices, with the system owner and security manager.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management sets migration priorities and funding

subtopics.isaca_rule: Quantum risk is a planning problem today. Start with an inventory, put long-lived secrets first and favor crypto agility. Public-key algorithms need replacing; symmetric encryption mainly needs long keys.

exam_traps.trap: Quantum computers will break all encryption, so AES must be replaced too.
exam_traps.why: The main threat is to public-key algorithms. AES with long keys and modern hashes are expected to stay secure.

exam_traps.trap: There is no risk until a quantum computer actually exists.
exam_traps.why: Data recorded today can be decrypted later, so long-lived secrets are already exposed.

key_terms.definition: Collecting encrypted data today to decrypt once quantum computing makes that possible.
The ability to swap cryptographic algorithms in a system without a major redesign.

subtopics.memory_aid: Public-key is at risk, symmetric holds: list it, rank it, swap it.

subtopics.name: Data Leakage into Public AI Services
subtopics.definition: Data leakage into public artificial intelligence (AI) services happens when people paste or upload sensitive information into an AI tool their organization does not control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A prompt is a data transfer. Depending on the terms, the provider may store it, read it or train models on it.
how_it_works: Typing data into a public AI chatbot sends it to a third party, like emailing an outside company.
An AI acceptable use policy names approved tools and the classification levels each may handle.
Approved enterprise tools have contracts limiting retention and training use; free public tools usually do not.
Data loss prevention (DLP) and web filtering can warn or block when labeled data heads to unapproved AI sites.
Accidental sharing is reported as a possible incident, because copies may already sit outside the organization.
subtopics.example: Taylor, a customer service agent at a utility company, pastes a customer's account and payment history into a free public chatbot to draft a reply, then remembers the AI policy. Instead of deleting the chat and saying nothing, Taylor reports it to the team lead and the security team.

review: Compare the task with the AI policy and approved tools list first
Remove sensitive details before using even an approved tool, where policy requires
evidence: The approved AI tools list, with each tool's data limits
DLP alerts for sensitive data sent to AI websites
audit_focus.recommend: Report sensitive data shared with an unapproved AI service to your supervisor and the security team at once.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves the AI policy and tools; data owners decide what data may be used

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat any public AI prompt as sharing data with an outsider. Use only approved AI tools, at the levels they are approved for, and report accidental sharing instead of hiding it.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting the chat history removes the data from the AI provider.
exam_traps.why: The provider may already have stored or logged copies. The exposure still needs reporting.

exam_traps.trap: Public AI tools are fine for confidential work once the customer's name is removed.
exam_traps.why: Account numbers, addresses or source code can still identify people or reveal secrets.

key_terms.definition: AI tools used for work without the organization's approval or oversight.
Rules for how staff may use organization systems and services, including AI tools.

topics.overview: Security operations is the daily watch over systems: collecting logs, spotting what matters among millions of events and deciding what to do. This topic also covers who attacks and why, common malware (malicious software), threat intelligence and frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK, and how AI can help or hurt alert triage.
can_do: Tell an event from an alert and an incident, and say when to escalate
Explain what to log, how to protect logs, and what a security information and event management (SIEM) system adds
Rank alerts by severity, asset value and confidence, and explain how correlation and AI cut noise
Match threat actors to motives, name common malware types, and explain how threat intelligence and ATT&CK help

subtopics.name: Events, Alerts and Incidents
subtopics.definition: An event is anything observable on a system or network; an alert flags an event for review; an incident actually or imminently harms security or violates policy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Treating every event as an incident swamps the response team; treating a real incident as routine lets damage spread.
how_it_works: Systems produce huge numbers of events every day, and nearly all are normal activity.
Monitoring rules turn a small share into alerts; an analyst checks each one and closes false alarms with a note.
The incident response plan defines what counts as an incident, with examples.
Declaring an incident starts the plan: the incident response team takes over, and severity sets who must be told.

types.meaning: Anything observable, such as a login, a file change or a blocked connection.
An event that a rule or tool flags for a person to review.
An occurrence that actually or imminently harms confidentiality, integrity or availability, or violates policy.
An incident in which data is confirmed to have been exposed to an unauthorized party.

subtopics.example: Overnight, a school district's monitoring tool alerts that a staff account logged in from two countries within an hour, then downloaded the payroll file. The plan lists this as an incident, so Jamie, the analyst on shift, stops investigating alone and escalates it, with notes, to the on-call incident response lead.

review: Compare what you see with the plan's incident definitions and examples
Write down what you checked before closing or escalating an alert
evidence: The alert's source, time, affected asset and account
Related events on the same host or account
audit_focus.recommend: Call the on-call incident response lead as soon as an event looks like an incident, or whenever you are unsure.
audit_focus.decides: The incident response lead declares incidents; legal counsel and management decide on notification

subtopics.isaca_rule: Not every event is an incident. Use the plan's definitions, record your reasoning, and hand anything over the threshold to the incident response team instead of carrying on alone.

exam_traps.trap: Every failed login or blocked connection should be reported as an incident.
exam_traps.why: These are normal events. Reporting them all floods the response team and hides real incidents.

exam_traps.trap: The analyst who finds exposed data should declare a breach and notify customers.
exam_traps.why: Notification is a legal decision with deadlines. Escalate the facts; legal counsel and management decide.

key_terms.definition: An event with a negative effect, such as a system crash; it may or may not become an incident.
The formal point at which an event is treated as an incident and the response plan starts.

subtopics.name: Logging and Monitoring
subtopics.definition: Logging records who did what, when, where and with what result; monitoring reviews those records, often in a central tool, to spot problems quickly.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without logs, attacks go unseen and investigations have no evidence. Logs nobody reviews, or that attackers can erase, give false comfort.
how_it_works: Useful entries record the user or process, the action, the time, the source and destination, and the result.
Every system syncs its clock to a trusted time source, so events from different logs line up.
Logs go to a central store that ordinary administrators cannot change, so intruders cannot cover their tracks.
A security information and event management (SIEM) system collects logs, normalizes them and applies rules to raise alerts.
subtopics.example: At a regional bank, a file server's security log is cleared overnight. Because the server also sends logs to the SIEM, Dana, a junior analyst in the security operations center, can still see that a new administrator account was created just before. Dana opens a ticket with these findings and escalates it.

review: Confirm each new system sends logs to the SIEM before it goes live
Investigate when a log source suddenly stops sending
evidence: Log source list showing which systems feed the SIEM
Time sync status across servers and network devices
audit_focus.recommend: Report cleared, altered or suddenly silent logs to the security operations lead as a possible sign of compromise.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides what is logged and how long logs are kept

subtopics.isaca_rule: Log what matters, sync every clock, and send logs somewhere the people being logged cannot alter them. A cleared or silent log is itself a warning sign to report.

exam_traps.trap: Turning on logging is enough; review can wait until something goes wrong.
exam_traps.why: Unreviewed logs detect nothing. Rules, alerts and regular review turn records into early warning.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping logs only on the server that creates them is fine if the server is secure.
exam_traps.why: An attacker with administrator rights can wipe local logs. A central, protected copy keeps the evidence.

key_terms.definition: The team that monitors and responds to security events; not the System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports in Domain 4.
Assurance that log records have not been altered or deleted, for example through write-once storage.

subtopics.name: Event Triage: Use Cases, Prioritization and Correlation
subtopics.definition: Event triage sorts incoming alerts to decide which are real, how urgent each is and who must act, using defined use cases, priority rules and correlation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A security operations center can receive thousands of alerts a day. Triage puts the dangerous few in front of analysts first, so a real attack is not lost in the noise.
how_it_works: A use case defines one thing to detect, such as many failed logins then a success, with its rule and response steps.
Priority weighs severity, the asset's value and confidence the alert is real: a payroll server outranks a test laptop.
Correlation links related events, such as a phishing email, a malware (malicious software) alert and an odd login, into one case.
Threats a tool already blocked are logged; events needing a human decision are escalated.

rows.label: What happens
cells: An alert fires on normal activity
A real attack raises no alert

rows.label: Cost
cells: Wasted analyst time and alert fatigue

rows.label: Usual fix
cells: Tune the rule so it fires less on normal activity
Add or improve the use case and its data sources

subtopics.example: A parcel company's console shows three alerts: a printer offline, a blocked internet port scan, and a domain administrator logging in at 3 a.m. from a warehouse kiosk it never uses. Lee, the analyst on duty, ranks the administrator login first and follows its playbook.

review: Rank open alerts with the priority matrix before starting work
Correlate each alert with recent events for the same user and host
evidence: Asset criticality and owner for the affected system
Recent related alerts across email, endpoint and login logs
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate high-priority or correlated alerts to the incident response team as the playbook directs.
audit_focus.decides: The security operations lead approves rule tuning and changes to priority rules

subtopics.isaca_rule: Triage by impact, not arrival order. Rank by severity, asset value and confidence, look for related events and follow the playbook. Close nothing without a reason.

exam_traps.trap: Handle alerts strictly in the order they arrive, so nothing is skipped.
exam_traps.why: A critical alert can wait behind dozens of trivial ones. Priority rules put the riskiest first.

exam_traps.trap: A rule that produces many false positives should be switched off.
exam_traps.why: That may hide a real attack. Tune the rule through the change process instead.

key_terms.definition: Linking related events across sources and time to reveal an attack that single events would not show.
Step-by-step instructions for handling a specific type of alert or incident.

subtopics.name: AI-Driven Correlation and Alert Fatigue
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) correlation uses machine learning to group, rank and summarize security alerts; alert fatigue is when too many alerts cause analysts to miss real ones.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Overloaded analysts close alerts on instinct, and real attacks slip past. AI cuts the noise, but trusted blindly or manipulated, it can hide what matters.
how_it_works: Machine learning in a security information and event management (SIEM) system groups related alerts into one case and removes duplicates.
It ranks cases by learned risk and can draft summaries, giving analysts a shorter, better-ordered queue.
Models can be wrong: aggressive suppression creates false negatives, and summaries can state facts the logs do not support.
People stay accountable: analysts check the evidence behind AI rankings, and suppression changes need approval.
subtopics.example: An airline's new AI-assisted SIEM cuts the daily queue from 4,000 alerts to 300 cases. A month later, Avery, a security analyst, finds it auto-closing logins from an unknown account on a baggage server. Avery does not change the model's settings; they escalate the suppression pattern to the security operations lead.

review: Open the raw events behind any AI-ranked case before closing it
Record cases where the AI ranking or summary was wrong
evidence: Alerts the AI suppressed or auto-closed during your shift
Detection test results showing whether known attacks still raise alerts
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected AI misses, signs of poisoning or unexplained suppression to the security operations lead.
audit_focus.decides: The security operations lead approves AI tuning and suppression changes

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI should shrink the queue, not replace judgment. Check the evidence behind its rankings, treat its summaries as leads, and report odd suppression instead of quietly overriding the tool.

exam_traps.trap: Once AI correlation is in place, analysts can trust its ranking without checking.
exam_traps.why: Rankings can be wrong or manipulated. Confirm the evidence, especially before closing a case as harmless.

exam_traps.trap: The cure for alert fatigue is to turn off most alert rules.
exam_traps.why: That trades noise for blindness. Tune rules, correlate alerts and test that real attacks still raise alerts.

key_terms.definition: Automatically hiding or closing low-value alerts; useful against noise, risky if it hides real attacks.
Tampering with the data a model learns from, so it learns to ignore certain activity.

subtopics.name: Threat Actors and Motives
subtopics.definition: A threat actor is a person or group that could harm an organization's systems or data; their motive, such as money, spying or protest, predicts what they target.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Actors want different things and have very different skills. Knowing who is likely to attack, and why, tells defenders what to protect first.
how_it_works: Actors differ in motive, skill, resources and whether they are inside or outside the organization.
Motive predicts the target: criminals seek payment data or ransom, spies seek secrets, activists seek publicity.
Insiders already have access; some act with intent, but many cause harm by mistake, such as misdirected emails.
Low-skill attackers use ready-made tools, yet still succeed against unpatched systems and weak passwords.

types.meaning: Government-linked groups seeking espionage or disruption, with the most skill and resources.
Groups seeking money through ransomware (malware that locks files for a ransom), fraud and selling stolen data.
Attackers driven by a political or social cause, often using defacement, leaks or denial of service.
Current or former staff, contractors or partners who misuse their access, deliberately or by accident.
Someone with little expertise using ready-made tools, often for thrills or notoriety.
A rival seeking trade secrets or advantage through industrial espionage.

subtopics.example: A small engineering firm wins a government contract to design a bridge component. Soon after, staff receive well-written emails, seemingly from the client, asking them to open design 'revisions'. Rowan, the firm's only security analyst, sees the pattern of an espionage-minded actor, reports it to the IT manager and drafts a staff phishing warning for approval.

review: Note the likely motive when you write up suspicious activity
Share relevant sector threat reports with your team when policy allows
evidence: Which assets attackers with each motive would most want
Signs of insider misuse, such as unusual downloads before someone leaves
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected insider activity quietly to your supervisor or the security lead, not to the person or coworkers.
audit_focus.decides: Management, with human resources and legal counsel, decides actions on suspected insiders

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask who would want this and why. Motive points to the likely target and method. Never assume the organization is too small to target: criminals and automated attacks hit everyone.

exam_traps.trap: Insider threats are always malicious employees.
exam_traps.why: Many insider incidents are mistakes, such as sending data to the wrong person. Controls aim at both careless and malicious insiders.

exam_traps.trap: Only nation-states are dangerous, so small organizations need not worry.
exam_traps.why: Criminals attack anyone with weak defenses, and small firms are often stepping stones into larger partners.

key_terms.definition: A skilled, well-funded attacker, often state-linked, that stays hidden in a network for a long time.
The path an attacker uses to reach a target, such as email, a web application or a removable drive.

subtopics.name: Cyber Threat Intelligence
subtopics.definition: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is threat information that has been collected, analyzed and put in context, so defenders can make better decisions about likely attacks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Raw threat data is noise until someone judges what matters here.
how_it_works: Sources include vendors, government agencies, open sources and sector groups called Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs).
Indicators of compromise, such as malicious file hashes, domains or Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, feed tools that block or detect known threats.
Indicators go stale quickly as attackers change infrastructure; knowledge of attacker methods stays useful longer.
Shared intelligence carries a Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) label, such as TLP:RED or TLP:CLEAR, saying how far it may travel.

types.meaning: High-level trends for leaders, such as which actors target the sector and why.
Details of specific campaigns: who is targeting the organization now, and how.
Attacker tactics, techniques and procedures, used to shape defenses and detections.
Specific indicators, such as hashes and addresses, used directly by security tools.

subtopics.example: A water utility's sector ISAC shares a TLP:AMBER report on ransomware entering utilities through an unpatched remote access appliance. Noor, a junior analyst, confirms the same appliance is in use and searches the logs for its indicators. Noor shares the report only as the label allows and briefs the security manager.

review: Search your logs and tools for indicators from new trusted reports
Keep the original TLP label on any intelligence you pass on
evidence: Whether products named in reports appear in your asset inventory
The age and source of indicators before blocking on them
audit_focus.recommend: Send intelligence that matches your environment to the security manager or incident response lead promptly.
audit_focus.decides: The security manager decides what to block and which systems to prioritize

subtopics.isaca_rule: Intelligence helps only when relevant, timely and acted on. Check it against your assets, feed indicators to your tools and respect sharing labels.

exam_traps.trap: More threat feeds always mean better security.
exam_traps.why: Unfiltered feeds add noise. Value comes from intelligence that fits your sector and assets and is acted on.

exam_traps.trap: A TLP:AMBER report can be posted to a public forum to warn others.
exam_traps.why: AMBER limits sharing to the recipient's organization and clients who need to know. Only TLP:CLEAR may be shared publicly.

key_terms.definition: Evidence that a system may have been breached, such as a known malicious file hash, domain or address.
A labeling scheme from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) setting how far shared information may travel.

subtopics.name: Threat Frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK and the Kill Chain
subtopics.definition: Threat frameworks describe attacks in a shared language: MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) catalogs real attacker methods; the Cyber Kill Chain orders attack stages.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A shared language lets analysts, tools and reports describe behavior the same way, and mapping defenses to it shows the detection gaps.
how_it_works: ATT&CK is a free knowledge base from the nonprofit MITRE, built from observed attacks.
Tactics are the attacker's goals, such as initial access; techniques are the ways each goal is reached, such as phishing.
Defenders map detections to techniques to find gaps; red teams use the same map to plan realistic tests.
The Cyber Kill Chain, from Lockheed Martin, has seven stages from reconnaissance to actions on objectives; breaking any link can stop the attack.

rows.label: Shape
cells: A matrix of tactics, each with many techniques
Seven stages in a fixed order

rows.label: Built from
cells: A model of how intrusions progress

rows.label: Best for
cells: Mapping detections and gaps in detail
Explaining an attack's flow and where to break it

rows.label: Limit
cells: Large; not a checklist to complete
Less detail; fits outside intrusions best

subtopics.example: After a phishing incident, a museum's security lead asks Quinn, a junior analyst, to map it to ATT&CK. Quinn lists each step against its tactic: the email (initial access), a malicious macro (execution), a scheduled task (persistence) and a large upload (exfiltration), then marks which steps raised no alert.

review: Tag alerts and incident notes with the matching ATT&CK technique
List which steps of a past attack were and were not detected
evidence: Coverage of techniques used by actors targeting your sector
Techniques that raised no alert during tests
audit_focus.recommend: Share the detection gaps you find with the security operations lead, with the evidence behind each one.
audit_focus.decides: The security operations lead decides which gaps to close first

subtopics.isaca_rule: Frameworks are maps, not checklists. Use them to describe attacks, find detection gaps and plan tests, focusing on the techniques your likely attackers actually use.

exam_traps.trap: MITRE ATT&CK is a compliance standard that must be fully implemented.
exam_traps.why: It is a knowledge base of attacker behavior, not a set of required controls. Organizations use it selectively.

exam_traps.trap: Tactics and techniques mean the same thing.
exam_traps.why: A tactic is the goal, the why; a technique is the method, the how. One tactic has many techniques.

key_terms.definition: How an attacker operates: goals, methods and a group's specific way of carrying them out.
A companion knowledge base (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) describing attacks on artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

subtopics.name: Malware Basics
subtopics.definition: Malware, short for malicious software, is any program written to harm a system or its users, such as by stealing data, locking files or handing control to an attacker.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Knowing how each kind spreads and what it does helps a practitioner spot the signs and take the right first step.
how_it_works: One attack often combines types, such as a Trojan that later installs ransomware.
Warning signs include slow or crashing systems, unknown programs, pop-ups, locked files and security tools switched off.
Patching, endpoint protection, email filtering and offline backups stop or limit most malware.
On finding malware: stop using the device, isolate it only as the playbook says, note what you saw and report at once.
Never run cleanup tools, wipe the device or answer a ransom demand; the incident response lead directs what happens next.

types.meaning: Attaches to a file or program and spreads when a person runs or shares it.
Spreads by itself across a network, usually through an unpatched flaw, with no user action.
Poses as useful software, so the user installs it and lets the attacker in.
Encrypts files, often after stealing them, then demands payment to unlock them or not leak them.
Secretly watches the user, such as recording keystrokes or stealing passwords and browsing data.
Hides deep in the operating system to keep an attacker's access and conceal other malware.

subtopics.example: At a hotel group, the monitoring tool flags a reception computer probing dozens of other machines, a sign of a worm. Imani, the IT technician on duty, follows the malware playbook: unplugs the network cable, leaves the computer running, photographs the screen and calls the incident response lead.

review: Compare odd device behavior with the playbook's list of malware signs
Confirm endpoint protection is running and current on devices you support
evidence: Endpoint protection alerts, with the file name, device and time
Devices whose protection is missing, disabled or out of date
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected malware at once through the incident channel, and wait for the incident response lead's direction.
audit_focus.decides: The incident response lead directs eradication; management, with legal counsel, decides on any ransom demand

subtopics.isaca_rule: Whatever the malware type, respond the same way: stop, isolate as the playbook allows, preserve and report. Never wipe, clean up or pay on your own.

exam_traps.trap: A virus and a worm are the same thing.
exam_traps.why: A virus needs a person to run an infected file; a worm spreads by itself through network flaws.

exam_traps.trap: Paying the ransom is the quickest safe way to get files back.
exam_traps.why: Payment does not guarantee working keys and may break sanctions law. Management decides with legal counsel; clean backups are the planned route.

key_terms.definition: Infected devices, called bots, that an attacker controls remotely, often for spam or denial-of-service attacks.
The channel an attacker uses to command infected devices and collect stolen data.

subtopics.memory_aid: A virus needs a ride, a worm walks alone, a Trojan wears a disguise.

topics.overview: Incident response is how an organization prepares for, detects, contains and recovers from incidents, then learns from them. This topic covers the plan and team, the response lifecycle and how current NIST guidance maps it to the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, handling evidence and data during a response, and exercises such as tabletops.
can_do: Put the incident response phases in order, and explain why containment comes before eradication
Match the classic lifecycle phases to the CSF 2.0 functions
Preserve evidence and keep a chain of custody while following the data handling policy
Choose the right exercise, such as a tabletop, to test an incident response plan

subtopics.name: The Incident Response Plan and Team
subtopics.definition: An incident response plan is the approved document that says what counts as an incident, who responds, what authority they have, how to communicate and which steps to follow.
subtopics.why_it_matters: In a crisis, people improvise, act alone or wait for permission. A plan approved in advance sets roles, authority and contacts, so the response is fast and coordinated.
how_it_works: Senior management approves the plan, giving the incident response team authority to act, such as isolating systems.
Severity levels set how fast to respond and who must be told.
Playbooks give step-by-step actions for common incidents, such as ransomware, phishing and lost devices.
Contact lists stay current, with after-hours numbers and an out-of-band channel in case email is compromised.
Everyone, not just the team, knows how to report a suspected incident.

types.meaning: Coordinates the response, makes operational decisions and keeps management informed.
Investigate, contain and eradicate the threat, and preserve evidence.
Advises on laws, contracts, evidence and notification duties.
Prepares approved messages for staff, customers, regulators and the media.
Approves major business decisions, such as shutting down a service or hiring outside help.

subtopics.example: Late on a Friday, Sky, an IT technician at a community college, sees ransom notes appearing on a shared drive. Sky's instinct is to start restoring files, but the plan says staff report first. Sky calls the on-call number, describes what they saw and when, and keeps notes.

review: Know the reporting number and channel before you ever need them
Report suspected incidents immediately, with what you saw and when
evidence: The current contact list and on-call schedule
Which playbook fits the situation you have found
audit_focus.recommend: Report anything that may be an incident through the plan's channel, even when unsure, then follow the incident response lead.
audit_focus.decides: The incident response lead directs the response; management approves major business decisions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Follow the plan, use the defined reporting path and act only within your role. Escalate early and let the incident response lead coordinate.

exam_traps.trap: An experienced technician should fix an incident quietly to avoid alarming management.
exam_traps.why: Quiet fixes skip evidence collection, notification duties and coordination. Report through the plan's path.

exam_traps.trap: Email is the best way to coordinate the response team.
exam_traps.why: If the attacker controls email, they can read the response as it unfolds. Use the plan's out-of-band channel.

key_terms.definition: Contact through a separate channel, such as phones, that an attacker inside the network cannot read.
The group responsible for handling incidents; in-house, outsourced or a mix.

subtopics.name: The Incident Response Lifecycle and CSF 2.0
subtopics.definition: The incident response lifecycle runs from preparation through detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery to lessons learned, which feed back into preparation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Steps out of order cause harm: wiping before containment lets the attacker carry on elsewhere, and restoring before eradication brings them back.
how_it_works: Preparation builds the plan, team, tools and training before anything happens.
Detection and analysis confirm an incident, judge its scope and severity, and start the record.
Containment stops the spread, eradication removes the cause, and recovery restores normal operations from known-good sources.
Lessons learned feed improvements back into the plan and controls.
NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, now maps this work to the six Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 functions.

rows.label: Get ready
cells: Govern, Identify and Protect: wider risk work that also prepares for incidents

rows.label: Improve
cells: Improvement, part of Identify: it happens all the time, not only at the end
