subtopics.example: Malware is found on a ferry company's ticketing server, and a sales manager wants it rebuilt from backup at once. Ellis, a systems administrator on the response team, reminds the incident response lead of the plan's order: contain and scope, remove the cause, check the backup predates the infection, then restore.

review: Confirm which phase the response is in before taking an action
Log each action with time, system and reason as you go
evidence: Scope of affected systems before anything is wiped or restored
Backup dates compared with the first sign of compromise
audit_focus.recommend: Raise pressure to skip a phase, such as restoring before eradication, with the incident response lead.
audit_focus.decides: The incident response lead decides when to move between phases

subtopics.isaca_rule: Order matters: contain before you eradicate, eradicate before you recover, and learn from every incident. The classic phases and the CSF 2.0 functions describe the same work.

exam_traps.trap: The first thing to do when malware is found is to wipe and rebuild the machine.
exam_traps.why: Wiping first destroys evidence and ignores other infected systems.

exam_traps.trap: The CSF-based model replaces the classic phases, so containment and eradication no longer apply.
exam_traps.why: The functions describe the same work at a higher level. Respond still includes containment and eradication; Recover restores operations.

key_terms.definition: A NIST framework, published in 2024, with six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
Which systems, accounts and data an incident affects; it must be known before eradication or recovery.

subtopics.memory_aid: Prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn: stop it before you scrub it.

subtopics.name: Containment, Eradication and Recovery
subtopics.definition: Containment stops an incident from spreading, eradication removes its cause, and recovery returns affected systems to normal, trusted operation, in that order.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Cleaning up before containing lets an attacker move elsewhere; restoring before eradication puts the attacker straight back.
how_it_works: Short-term containment acts fast, such as isolating an infected laptop or disabling a compromised account.
Isolating a running machine, rather than powering it off, usually keeps memory evidence; the playbook may say otherwise for some threats.
Eradication removes malware and attacker accounts, closes the exploited weakness and resets exposed credentials on every affected system.
Recovery restores from known-good backups or clean builds, patches them, then watches closely for a return.
subtopics.example: At a dental practice group, an office manager reports pop-ups and locked files on a reception computer. Robin, the IT support technician, follows the ransomware playbook's first steps: unplug the network cable, leave the computer on and call the incident response lead. Robin runs no cleanup tools until the lead confirms the scope.

review: Isolate the affected system as the playbook directs, leaving it running
Reset or disable exposed credentials only as the incident response lead directs
evidence: Other systems showing the same indicators
Backup dates against the earliest sign of compromise
audit_focus.recommend: Hand over to the incident response lead before running cleanup tools, wiping or restoring anything.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner, advised by the incident response lead, approves the return to service

subtopics.isaca_rule: Contain first, then eradicate, then recover. Isolate rather than power off unless the playbook says otherwise, remove every trace of the cause, and restore only from clean sources.

exam_traps.trap: Powering off an infected computer is the safest first step.
exam_traps.why: Powering off can erase memory evidence, such as running malware and open connections. Isolating it usually stops the spread and keeps evidence.

exam_traps.trap: Once malware is removed from the first infected laptop, the incident is over.
exam_traps.why: Attackers often spread or leave hidden access elsewhere. Eradication covers every affected system and the original weakness.

key_terms.definition: A backup taken before the compromise and confirmed clean, so restoring it does not bring the threat back.
Ways an attacker keeps access after a reboot or cleanup, such as hidden accounts or scheduled tasks.

subtopics.name: Evidence Handling and Chain of Custody
subtopics.definition: Evidence handling keeps digital and physical evidence reliable; chain of custody records everyone who handled it, when and why, from collection onward.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Incidents can lead to discipline, insurance claims or court, where evidence that cannot be shown untouched may be rejected.
how_it_works: Volatile evidence, such as memory and network connections, is collected before disk contents that survive a shutdown.
Investigators work on verified copies, called forensic images, and keep the original sealed.
A hash taken at collection that matches a later hash shows the evidence has not changed.
Every transfer is logged with date, time, names, purpose and storage location, and evidence is locked away.
Entry-level staff preserve the scene and report; trained forensic staff, guided by legal counsel, collect and analyze.
subtopics.example: A warehouse supervisor finds an unfamiliar memory stick in the back of a payroll computer. Pat, a security technician, photographs it in place, opens no files and calls the incident response lead. When the forensic investigator arrives, Pat hands over the photos and notes, and the handover is logged on the custody form.

review: Leave the device as found and note its state, time and location
Record every action you take on affected systems
evidence: Custody records with a name, time and reason for every handoff
Hash values recorded at collection and at each analysis
audit_focus.recommend: Call the incident response lead before touching suspected evidence, and let trained forensic staff collect it.
audit_focus.decides: Legal counsel and the incident response lead decide how evidence is collected and kept

subtopics.isaca_rule: Preserve first, analyze later, and only within your role. Do not browse, copy or clean a suspect device. Write down what you saw and did, and record every handoff.

exam_traps.trap: The analyst should open the suspicious files right away to see what they contain.
exam_traps.why: Opening files changes timestamps and may run malware. Preserve the device and let trained staff analyze a forensic copy.

exam_traps.trap: Chain of custody matters only if the police are already involved.
exam_traps.why: Many incidents become legal or disciplinary cases later, and custody cannot be rebuilt afterward.

key_terms.definition: Collecting the evidence that disappears fastest first, such as memory, then disk, then backups.
A device or tool that lets investigators read a drive without changing any data on it.

subtopics.name: Data Handling During an Incident
subtopics.definition: Data handling during an incident applies the organization's classification and handling rules to everything the response touches, including evidence, logs, reports and messages.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Response copies of disks, logs and records can hold the very data the attacker wanted. Mishandling them, or speaking too soon, can cause a second breach.
how_it_works: Evidence and incident reports take the classification of the most sensitive data they contain.
Details are shared on a need-to-know basis through approved channels, never personal email or chat apps.
The incident record notes which data types were affected, such as personal or payment data, because that drives legal duties.
Only designated roles, such as communications and legal counsel, speak to customers, regulators or the media.
subtopics.example: During a suspected data theft at a travel agency, a reporter calls asking whether customer passport details were exposed. A colleague asks Leah, a junior analyst helping the response, to 'just tell them it isn't true'. Leah declines, takes the reporter's details for the communications lead and keeps working only in the restricted case folder.

review: Store incident files only in the approved restricted case location
Refer outside questions to the designated spokesperson
evidence: Data types and classification levels the incident involves
Access lists on the case folder, limited to named responders
audit_focus.recommend: Tell the incident response lead at once if personal, health or payment data may be involved.
audit_focus.decides: Legal counsel and management decide notifications and public statements

subtopics.isaca_rule: During a response, handling rules get stricter, not looser. Keep incident data in approved restricted places, share on a need-to-know basis, and leave statements to the roles the plan names.

exam_traps.trap: In an emergency, it is fine to send logs to a personal email account to keep working from home.
exam_traps.why: Logs can hold sensitive data. Sending them outside approved systems creates a new exposure, emergency or not.

exam_traps.trap: A responder who knows the facts should reassure customers directly.
exam_traps.why: Early statements may be wrong and create legal risk. Refer questions to the named spokesperson.

key_terms.definition: Sharing information only with people who require it to do their part in the response.
A legal or contractual duty to tell affected people, regulators or partners about certain breaches within set deadlines.

subtopics.name: Lessons Learned and Continuous Improvement
subtopics.definition: Lessons learned is the review after an incident or exercise that asks what happened, what worked, what did not and what to change, then tracks the changes to completion.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a review, the same weakness causes the next incident. Improvements also keep the plan current as systems, threats and people change.
how_it_works: The review happens soon after the incident, while memories are fresh, with everyone who took part.
It is blameless: it looks for gaps in process, tools and training, not someone to punish, so people speak openly.
Findings become actions with owners and deadlines, such as a playbook update or a new detection.
Current NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) guidance treats improvement as continuous: share a lesson as soon as it is found.
subtopics.example: Two weeks after a phishing attack at a nonprofit, the incident response lead holds a review. Drew, the help desk technician, explains that three staff called about the strange email an hour before anyone told security, because the help desk script had no reporting step. The group adds one, owned by Drew's manager.

review: Bring your timeline notes and observations to the review
Complete improvement actions assigned to you and report progress
evidence: Open improvement actions and their due dates
Whether the same root cause appeared in earlier incidents
audit_focus.recommend: Raise overdue or unowned improvement actions with the incident response lead or your manager.
audit_focus.decides: Management approves and funds the improvements

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every incident and exercise should change something. Speak honestly in reviews, focus on process rather than blame, and make sure each improvement has an owner and a due date.

exam_traps.trap: The main goal of the review is to find out who was at fault.
exam_traps.why: Blame makes people hide mistakes and early warnings. Reviews look for process and control gaps.

exam_traps.trap: A small incident does not need a lessons learned review.
exam_traps.why: Small incidents often reveal the same gaps as big ones, at lower cost.

key_terms.definition: A written summary of an incident or exercise: its timeline, findings and agreed actions.
The underlying reason an incident happened, such as a missing patch, rather than its symptoms.

subtopics.name: Incident Response Exercises and Tabletops
subtopics.definition: Incident response exercises test the plan and the people before a real incident, ranging from discussion-based tabletops to hands-on, full-scale exercises.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A plan nobody has practiced fails under pressure: numbers are wrong, roles unclear and decisions stall. Exercises find these gaps while mistakes cost nothing.
how_it_works: Each exercise has objectives, a realistic scenario and an agreed scope, so it does not disrupt real operations.
A facilitator presents the scenario in stages, adding new facts called injects to test decisions.
The exercise ends with a debrief and an after-action report, and findings feed lessons learned.
Exercises repeat regularly and after major changes, and can include cloud providers, legal counsel and insurers.
Continuity and recovery plan tests use their own ladder, ending in parallel and full interruption tests that move real operations.

types.meaning: A discussion-based session where the team talks through its response; no systems are touched.
A focused practice of one task, such as calling the contact list.
Teams carry out their roles in a simulated environment, under time pressure, without touching production.
Many teams, sometimes with outside partners, respond as close to real operations as is safe.

subtopics.example: A food distribution company runs its first ransomware tabletop. Halfway through, the facilitator adds an inject: email is down. The team realizes nobody has the incident response lead's mobile number, and the contact list lives only in email. Mika, the junior analyst taking notes, records the gap for the after-action report.

review: Play the role you would hold in a real incident
Note anything unclear in your instructions or contacts
evidence: Your assigned role and the contact list you would use
After-action items assigned to your team
audit_focus.recommend: Report gaps you notice during an exercise to the facilitator or exercise lead, even if they seem minor.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets the exercise schedule and approves the resulting changes

subtopics.isaca_rule: Practice before you need it. Start with tabletops to check roles and decisions, move to hands-on exercises as the plan matures, and treat every gap found as a success.

exam_traps.trap: A tabletop exercise proves that systems can actually be restored.
exam_traps.why: Tabletops are discussions that test roles and decisions. Proving recovery needs a hands-on test, such as a restore test.

exam_traps.trap: An exercise is needed only once, when the plan is first written.
exam_traps.why: People, systems and threats change, so exercises repeat regularly and after major changes.

key_terms.definition: A new piece of scenario information added during an exercise to test how the team adapts.
The person who runs an exercise, presents the scenario and keeps discussion on its objectives.

topics.overview: You cannot protect what you do not know you have. This topic covers an inventory of hardware, software, data, cloud and AI assets with named owners, managing each asset from purchase to disposal, handling end-of-life systems, and keeping systems in a secure, known state through configuration, patch and change management.
can_do: Explain why an accurate asset inventory with named owners comes first
Choose a safe option for end-of-life software or devices that can no longer be patched
Describe secure baselines, configuration drift and how patches are prioritized and tested
Follow the change management steps, including for emergency changes

subtopics.name: Asset Inventory and Ownership
subtopics.definition: An asset inventory is an up-to-date list of hardware, software, data, cloud services and artificial intelligence (AI) assets, each with a named owner.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unknown assets are not patched, monitored or backed up, so attackers often get in through them. The inventory underpins nearly every other control.
how_it_works: Discovery tools scan networks and cloud accounts, and the results are matched against purchase records.
Each entry records the owner, location, criticality, data handled and support status.
AI assets include models, training data, prompts and outside AI services, tracked like any other asset.
Unknown devices or services are investigated, then brought under management or removed through procedure.
subtopics.example: A network scan at an elementary school finds a device nobody recognizes: an old camera recorder still using its factory password. Jesse, the IT technician, adds it to the inventory, asks the facilities manager to confirm ownership, and logs the default password as a finding for the owner to fix.

review: Add new assets to the inventory before or as they are deployed
Investigate unknown devices that discovery scans find
evidence: Discovery results compared with the inventory for unlisted assets
Inventory entries missing an owner or a support end date
audit_focus.recommend: Report unknown or unowned assets to your supervisor so that an owner can be assigned.
audit_focus.decides: The asset owner decides how the asset is used and accepts its risks

subtopics.isaca_rule: Inventory comes first: every asset needs an entry and an owner. When you find something unknown, record it and find its owner instead of ignoring it or unplugging it yourself.

exam_traps.trap: Whoever finds an unknown device on the network should unplug it immediately.
exam_traps.why: It may run a business process, such as cameras or medical equipment. Report it; isolate it at once only if it is actively harmful and procedure allows.

exam_traps.trap: The asset inventory needs to list only hardware.
exam_traps.why: Software, data, cloud services and AI models are assets too, and each needs an owner and protection.

key_terms.definition: Technology used for work without IT or security approval, such as unapproved cloud apps.
A central record of assets, their settings and how they connect, used in change and incident work.

subtopics.name: The Asset Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: The asset lifecycle covers each stage of an asset's life, from planning and buying through deployment, operation and maintenance to retirement and secure disposal.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security problems are cheapest to avoid early and easiest to forget at the end. A device bought without requirements, or discarded unsanitized, can expose data for years.
how_it_works: Acquisition sets security requirements, such as encryption and vendor patch support, before anything is bought.
Deployment applies the secure baseline, records the asset and assigns its owner.
Operation keeps the asset, including artificial intelligence (AI) tools and models, patched, monitored and backed up, changed only through change management.
Retirement removes the asset from access lists, firewall rules and monitoring.
Disposal sanitizes or destroys storage and records the result, including for leased or returned equipment.
subtopics.example: A grocery chain boxes its old warehouse handheld scanners for a recycler. Kim, an IT technician, notices they still hold cached delivery addresses and saved Wi-Fi passwords. Kim pauses the shipment, tells the asset manager, and sanitizes and records each device as the disposal procedure requires.

review: Follow the disposal procedure for every retired device, including small ones
Remove retired assets from monitoring, access lists and the inventory
evidence: Disposal records matched against assets marked as retired
Leased or returned equipment still waiting for sanitization
audit_focus.recommend: Report any asset about to leave the organization without sanitization records to the asset manager.
audit_focus.decides: The asset owner approves retirement; policy sets the disposal method

subtopics.isaca_rule: Security belongs at every stage. Build requirements in before purchase, and close out properly at the end: sanitize, update the records and remove access.

exam_traps.trap: Security starts once a system is installed.
exam_traps.why: Requirements set at purchase decide whether a product can be secured and patched at all. Fixing a poor choice later costs far more.

exam_traps.trap: A retired server can stay switched off in the rack until someone has time for it.
exam_traps.why: It still holds data and may still have accounts and network access. Decommission and dispose of it through the process.

key_terms.definition: Conditions a product must meet before purchase, such as patch support, encryption and logging.
Formally taking an asset out of service, including removing its accounts, network access and monitoring.

subtopics.name: End-of-Life Software and Devices
subtopics.definition: End-of-life (EOL) software or hardware no longer gets vendor support, including security patches, so newly found weaknesses stay unfixed for good.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers seek out unsupported products because every new flaw stays open, and these systems often run important processes.
how_it_works: Vendors announce end-of-support dates in advance; for security, the key date is when patches stop.
The inventory tracks support dates, so owners can plan upgrades in time.
The preferred fix is to upgrade or replace the system before support ends.
If that is not yet possible, reduce exposure: isolate it on its own network segment, limit access, monitor it closely or buy extended support.
Keeping it running needs a documented exception with an expiry date and a review.
subtopics.example: A clinic's ultrasound machine runs an operating system that lost support last year, and its maker will not approve an upgrade for two years. Ari, a junior network administrator, records it as end-of-life, proposes isolating it so only the imaging workstation can reach it, and sends the proposal to the clinic manager, the risk owner.

review: Flag assets whose support ends within the next year
Propose compensating controls when an EOL system cannot be replaced yet
evidence: Inventory report of assets past or near their support end
Exceptions for EOL systems, with their expiry and review dates
audit_focus.recommend: Send EOL findings to the asset owner and security manager, with the support end date and the data at risk.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts the remaining risk; the policy owner approves a time-limited exception

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan for end of support before it arrives. Upgrade or replace when you can; when you cannot, isolate, restrict and monitor under a documented, time-limited exception.

exam_traps.trap: If an unsupported system still works, it is safe to leave as is.
exam_traps.why: Working is not the same as secure. Every flaw found after support ends stays open.

exam_traps.trap: An analyst should switch off an unsupported machine as soon as they find it.
exam_traps.why: It may run a critical or life-safety process. Record and report it; the owner decides on replacement or compensating controls.

key_terms.definition: An alternative safeguard, such as network isolation, used when the normal control, such as patching, is not possible.
A documented, time-limited approval from the policy owner to operate outside a policy, reviewed before it expires.

subtopics.name: Configuration Management and Secure Baselines
subtopics.definition: Configuration management keeps systems in a known, approved state by defining secure baselines, applying them consistently, and detecting and correcting drift from them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Defaults are built for easy setup, and attackers know them. Without baselines, every system differs and weaknesses hide.
how_it_works: A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration for one type of system, such as a laptop, firewall or artificial intelligence (AI) service.
Hardening removes unneeded services, ports, accounts and software, and changes default passwords and settings.
Many organizations start from published guides, such as the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks, and adapt them.
Tools apply the baseline to new systems and scan existing ones for drift, such as a disabled firewall.
Drift is corrected or approved as a change; the baseline itself changes only through change management.
subtopics.example: A monthly scan at a housing association shows twelve laptops with disk encryption turned off, against the baseline. Fran, a desktop support technician, finds a contractor disabled it to speed up an install. Fran opens a ticket, re-enables encryption with the approved tool, and reports the cause to the desktop team lead.

review: Build new systems from the approved baseline image or template
Return drifted settings to the baseline with approved tools
evidence: Drift scan results against the current baseline
Hardening checklist results for each new build
audit_focus.recommend: Report repeated drift, or a baseline setting that blocks business work, to your team lead for a formal change.
audit_focus.decides: Security management approves the baseline standard; system owners apply it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Start every system from an approved baseline and treat any difference as a question: approved change or drift? Return drift to the baseline, and change the baseline only through change management.

exam_traps.trap: Default settings from a reputable vendor are secure enough to deploy.
exam_traps.why: Defaults favor easy setup and are publicly known, including default passwords. Harden to the baseline before go-live.

exam_traps.trap: A system that passed the baseline check at deployment stays compliant.
exam_traps.why: Updates, troubleshooting and quick fixes cause drift. Regular scans catch it.

key_terms.definition: Gradual, often unapproved changes that move a system away from its approved baseline.
All the points where an attacker could try to get in, such as open ports, services and accounts.

subtopics.name: Patch Management
subtopics.definition: Patch management finds, tests, approves and installs software updates that fix flaws, then confirms they worked, across every system in the inventory.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many breaches use flaws that already had a patch. Patching quickly closes those doors, but careless patching can break critical systems, so speed and testing are balanced.
how_it_works: Vendor notices and vulnerability scans show which systems need which patches.
Priority follows risk: the flaw's severity, whether attackers are exploiting it, and how exposed and critical the system is.
Patches are tested first, then deployed through change management with a rollback plan.
Urgent patches for actively exploited flaws use the emergency change route: faster, but still recorded.
Rescans confirm each patch; systems that cannot be patched get compensating controls and an exception.
subtopics.example: A vendor fixes a flaw in a file transfer product that attackers are already exploiting, and a pharmacy chain runs it on an internet-facing server. Devon, a systems administrator, confirms the server is affected and raises an emergency change. After a quick test and the change manager's approval, Devon patches and rescans.

review: Match each new patch to affected systems in the inventory
Confirm installation with a rescan after deployment
evidence: Patch compliance reports showing missing patches by system
Whether a flaw appears on an exploited-vulnerabilities list
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any actively exploited flaw on an exposed system with your team lead the same day.
audit_focus.decides: The change manager or change advisory board approves deployment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Patch by risk, not habit: actively exploited flaws on exposed, critical systems come first. Test, use the change process, even its emergency route, and verify.

exam_traps.trap: Install every patch on production systems the moment it is released.
exam_traps.why: Untested patches can break critical services. Test first, and use the emergency route when risk demands speed.

exam_traps.trap: Patches can wait for the quarterly cycle, whatever the flaw.
exam_traps.why: Actively exploited flaws on exposed systems need fast action. Priority follows risk, not the calendar.

key_terms.definition: A public list, kept by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, of flaws confirmed as exploited in real attacks.
A flaw that attackers exploit before the vendor has released a fix.

subtopics.name: Change Management
subtopics.definition: Change management is the controlled process for requesting, assessing, approving, testing, making and reviewing changes to systems, so changes do not cause outages or security gaps.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unplanned, untested changes are a leading cause of outages, and an unapproved change can quietly open a security hole.
how_it_works: A change request states what will change and why, the risk, the test plan and the rollback plan.
Someone other than the person making the change approves it.
Approved changes are tested, scheduled, made and checked, and configuration records are updated.
Emergency changes get fast approval from a designated person, then are recorded and reviewed soon after.
Changes found without approval are treated as possible incidents until explained.
subtopics.example: A finance manager at a construction firm asks Jo, a network technician, to open a firewall port at once so a supplier can upload invoices. There is no approval. Jo raises a change request with the port, the supplier's addresses and a rollback plan, and tells the manager the approver can fast-track urgent requests.

review: Raise a change request before changing any production system
Wait for recorded approval before starting, even under pressure
evidence: The change calendar for conflicts before scheduling work
Unapproved changes found in configuration or drift reports
audit_focus.recommend: Report pressure to make an unapproved change, or an unexplained change you find, to your supervisor or the change manager.
audit_focus.decides: The change advisory board or designated approver authorizes the change

subtopics.isaca_rule: No change without approval, testing and a way back. Urgency changes how fast approval happens, not whether it happens.

exam_traps.trap: Emergency changes skip the change process entirely.
exam_traps.why: They use a faster route with a designated approver, but are still recorded and reviewed afterward.

exam_traps.trap: A small configuration change by a senior engineer needs no approval.
exam_traps.why: Small changes can cause big outages. Seniority does not replace review, testing and a rollback plan.

key_terms.definition: A group that reviews and approves significant changes, weighing business, technical and security impact.
Steps prepared in advance to undo a change if it fails or causes problems.

topics.overview: Security testing checks whether defenses work before an attacker finds out they do not. This topic covers red, blue and purple teams, vulnerability scanning and penetration testing, static and dynamic application testing, threat modeling, physical and social engineering tests, and testing defenses that rely on AI. Every test needs written authorization and an agreed scope.
can_do: Tell a vulnerability scan from a penetration test, and tell red, blue and purple teams apart
Explain where static analysis, dynamic analysis and threat modeling fit in development
Describe phishing, tailgating and impersonation tests and the authorization each needs
Explain how to test a defense that relies on AI, including against prompt injection

subtopics.name: Red, Blue and Purple Teams
subtopics.definition: A red team plays the attacker, a blue team defends and detects, and a purple team is red and blue working together to improve detection and response.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Defenses that are never challenged give false confidence. Realistic attacks show whether people, processes and tools actually detect and stop what real attackers do.
how_it_works: Red teams copy known attacker techniques to reach agreed goals, such as reading a test file in the payroll system.
Blue teams, usually the security operations center, defend as normal and may not know a test is running.
In purple teaming, red shares each step as it happens, so blue can confirm detection and close gaps at once.
A white team sets the rules, referees and can stop the exercise if something goes wrong.

rows.label: Role
cells: Combines both, sharing in real time

rows.label: Main goal
cells: Show how far an attacker could get

rows.label: Typical output
cells: Alerts, response actions and noted gaps

subtopics.example: A bank's red team has two weeks to try to reach a test payments account. On day three, Sasha, a blue team analyst, spots an unusual login and escalates it as procedure requires. The white team confirms the test; afterward, red and blue fix the two techniques that went unseen.

review: Respond to suspicious activity normally, even during a known test period
Record which test steps you detected and how
evidence: The authorization letter and scope before joining any test
Detection results from the joint debrief
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate suspected test activity through normal channels and let the white team confirm it.
audit_focus.decides: Management authorizes the test and its scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Testing is legitimate only with written authorization, a clear scope and rules of engagement. Blue team staff treat anything suspicious as real; confirming a test is the white team's job.

exam_traps.trap: A blue team analyst who suspects a test should ignore the activity.
exam_traps.why: Real attackers count on that assumption. Follow normal procedure; the white team confirms tests.

exam_traps.trap: A purple team is a separate third team that attacks and defends at once.
exam_traps.why: Purple teaming is a way of working: red and blue share findings in real time.

key_terms.definition: The agreed limits of a test: targets, methods, timing, contacts and what testers must never do.
Testing that copies a specific threat actor's known behavior.

subtopics.name: Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing
subtopics.definition: A vulnerability scan uses automated tools to find known weaknesses; a penetration test is an authorized, mostly manual attempt to exploit weaknesses to show real impact.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Scans show what might be wrong; penetration tests show what an attacker could actually do. A clean scan does not prove safety.
how_it_works: Scans compare systems with databases of known flaws, producing long lists that need checking for false positives.
Penetration testers chain weaknesses together to prove impact, within an agreed scope and time window.
Findings are ranked with the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), now version 4.0, plus asset value and active exploitation.
Both need the system owner's approval, and fixes are verified by rescanning or retesting.

rows.label: Exploits flaws?
cells: Generally no; it identifies and reports them

rows.label: Answers
cells: What could an attacker actually achieve?

subtopics.example: A retailer's monthly scan reports 600 findings, and a manager asks whether that counts as the penetration test. Lou, a junior security analyst, explains that the scan listed possible weaknesses without trying to exploit them, then sends the critical findings on internet-facing systems to their owners first.

review: Run scans only against systems in the approved scope
Check high findings for false positives before assigning them
evidence: Scan coverage compared with the asset inventory
Rescan results confirming that fixes worked
audit_focus.recommend: Send critical findings on exposed systems to the system owner and your team lead promptly.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner approves testing and decides how to treat each finding

subtopics.isaca_rule: A scan finds known weaknesses; a penetration test proves what they allow. Both need the owner's approval. A CVSS score measures severity, not your risk: also weigh exploitation, asset value and exposure.

exam_traps.trap: Running a vulnerability scanner counts as a penetration test.
exam_traps.why: Scanners identify possible weaknesses but do not exploit or chain them. A penetration test shows actual impact.

exam_traps.trap: An analyst may scan a partner's systems to check their security, as long as nothing is damaged.
exam_traps.why: Testing systems you do not own without written permission can be illegal. Get the owner's authorization first.

key_terms.definition: A public catalog giving each known vulnerability a unique identifier, in the form CVE-year-number.
A scan that logs in to each system, so it can see missing patches and settings an outsider cannot.

subtopics.name: Static and Dynamic Application Testing
subtopics.definition: Static application security testing (SAST) examines source code without running it; dynamic application security testing (DAST) probes the running application from outside, as an attacker would.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Flaws are cheapest to fix while code is written and dearest in production. Each method finds problems the other misses, so applications need both.
how_it_works: SAST runs early, often in the developer's tools or build pipeline, and points to the exact line of code.
SAST can flag issues that are not exploitable, so developers review its results.
DAST tests a running copy, usually in a test environment, and finds runtime and configuration problems such as weak session handling.
Software composition analysis (SCA) checks third-party libraries for known flaws.
Many teams test against the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 list of web application risks.

rows.label: When
cells: Early, while code is written and built
Later, once a working version exists

rows.label: Finds well
cells: Coding flaws, such as unsafe input handling

rows.label: Limits
cells: Cannot point to the faulty line of code

subtopics.example: A transit agency is about to launch a fare top-up website. The SAST report is clean, so the project manager wants to skip the scheduled DAST run to save a week. Nico, a junior application security analyst, explains that SAST cannot see live session handling or server settings, and asks to keep the run, as policy requires.

review: Review SAST findings with developers before marking any as false positives
Run DAST only against approved test environments
evidence: Critical findings still open before each release
Library versions flagged as vulnerable in the dependency report
audit_focus.recommend: Raise releases planned with unresolved critical findings to the application owner and security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The application owner decides on release, accepting any remaining risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Use both: SAST early on the code, DAST later on the running application, plus checks on third-party components. A clean result from one does not cover the other's blind spots.

exam_traps.trap: A clean SAST report means the web application is secure.
exam_traps.why: SAST cannot see runtime behavior or server settings. DAST and other testing cover those.

exam_traps.trap: DAST is best run early, before any code compiles.
exam_traps.why: DAST needs a running application. Early on, SAST and code review are the tools that fit.

key_terms.definition: Moving security testing earlier in development, where fixes are cheaper and faster.
Testing with no knowledge of the internal code or design, as an outside attacker would.

subtopics.name: Threat Modeling
subtopics.definition: Threat modeling is a structured way to find what could go wrong with a system's design, rank those threats, and choose defenses before the system is built or changed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Design flaws are costly to fix after building. Thinking like an attacker at the whiteboard finds them early.
how_it_works: A simple approach asks four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, and did we do a good job?
Teams draw a data flow diagram showing components, data stores, flows and trust boundaries.
STRIDE, named for the six threat types below, prompts the team at each part of the diagram.
Each threat gets a response: a control, a design change, or documented acceptance by the risk owner.

types.meaning: Pretending to be someone or something else; countered by authentication.
Changing data or code without permission; countered by integrity controls.
Denying an action when there is no way to prove it; countered by logging and signatures.
Exposing data to people not allowed to see it; countered by encryption and access control.
Making a system unavailable; countered by capacity planning and filtering.
Gaining rights beyond those granted; countered by authorization checks and least privilege.

subtopics.example: A small charity plans an online donation form. In a one-hour session, Bailey, the junior security analyst, walks the team through the data flow and asks what could go wrong at each step. The team sees card details would pass through the charity's own server and redesigns the form around the payment provider's hosted page.

review: Join design reviews and ask what could go wrong at each trust boundary
Write down every threat in the threat log with its agreed response
evidence: A data flow diagram that matches the design being built
Threats left open without an owner-approved response
audit_focus.recommend: Raise high-risk design threats that have no agreed response with the system owner and security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides how each threat is treated

subtopics.isaca_rule: Find design threats before building, when fixes are cheapest. Draw the system, look hardest at trust boundaries, use a prompt list such as STRIDE, and give every threat an approved response.

exam_traps.trap: Threat modeling is done once the system is finished, as a final check.
exam_traps.why: It is most valuable during design, when changes are cheap.

exam_traps.trap: Threat modeling is a job for expert penetration testers only.
exam_traps.why: It works best with the people who design, build and run the system. Simple methods make it practical for whole teams.

key_terms.definition: A point where data or control passes between parts of a system with different levels of trust.
A simple drawing of how data moves between users, processes and data stores in a system.

subtopics.name: Physical and Social Engineering Penetration Tests
subtopics.definition: Physical and social engineering penetration tests check, with written permission, whether people and premises resist tricks such as phishing, tailgating and impersonation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers often find people and doors easier than firewalls. These tests show whether staff challenge strangers and report suspicious messages.
how_it_works: Phishing simulations send realistic but harmless emails and measure who clicks and, more importantly, who reports.
Tailgating and piggybacking tests check whether a tester can slip in behind staff unnoticed, or be let in without a badge.
Impersonation tests use a pretext, such as a delivery driver or IT contractor, to see whether staff verify identity.
Testers carry a signed authorization letter and stop if anyone's safety is at risk.

types.meaning: Deceptive messages that try to get people to click a link, open a file or give away credentials.
An unauthorized person follows someone through a controlled door without that person's knowledge or consent.
An unauthorized person follows someone through a controlled door with that person's knowledge or consent, such as when they hold it open.
Pretending to be a trusted person, such as a vendor, coworker or inspector, to gain access or information.

subtopics.example: Jun, a records clerk at a government office, hears someone catch the records room door behind them: a person in a high-visibility vest, there 'to fix the air conditioning'. Jun politely walks them to reception to sign in and reports the tailgating attempt. It was an authorized test, and Jun's report counts as the right response.

review: Challenge or redirect anyone without a visible badge in secure areas
Report suspicious emails with the report button rather than just deleting them
evidence: Visitor sign-in and escort procedures at your site
Phishing report rates and speed after each simulation
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected tailgating or impersonation to the security team immediately, even if you think it may be a test.
audit_focus.decides: Management authorizes physical and social engineering tests and their scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Be courteous but verify: no badge, no entry, and confirm identity through a known channel, not the person's own story. Report it even if it may be a test.

exam_traps.trap: Holding a secure door for a friendly stranger carrying boxes is polite and harmless.
exam_traps.why: Knowingly letting them in is piggybacking. Ask them to badge in, or send them to reception to be verified and escorted.

exam_traps.trap: To keep results realistic, the security team can run a surprise phishing test without telling management.
exam_traps.why: Every test needs written authorization and an agreed scope from management, even internal ones. Unauthorized tests can breach policy, privacy rules and staff trust.

key_terms.definition: A made-up story or role an attacker uses to make a request seem legitimate.
A signed management document allowing specified tests within a set scope and period.

subtopics.name: Testing AI-Integrated Defenses
subtopics.definition: Testing AI-integrated defenses checks whether security tools that rely on artificial intelligence (AI) can be fooled, manipulated or made to fail, and whether people can override them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI now filters email and ranks alerts. If an attacker can trick the model, the defense fails silently.
how_it_works: Testers try known AI attacks and check whether other defenses catch what the model misses.
Red teams replay attacks after each model update to confirm the detector still alerts.
Testers confirm the AI has only the access it needs, logs its actions and lets a person stop high-impact actions.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 for large language model (LLM) applications describes many of these attacks.

types.meaning: Instructions hidden in input, or in content the AI reads, aimed at overriding its rules or extracting data.
Slightly altered inputs, such as a reworded phishing email, designed to slip past an AI detector.
Tainting the data a model learns from so that it misclassifies certain attacks.
An AI tool given more permissions or autonomy than it needs, so a manipulated model can do real damage.

subtopics.example: A law firm adds an AI assistant that summarizes incoming email. During an authorized test, Remy, a junior security analyst, sends an email with hidden text telling the assistant to forward the client list outside the firm. The assistant tries, but its permissions block sending. Remy records the result and reports the weakness to the application owner.

review: Test AI features only within the approved scope and test accounts
Record each test input, the AI's response and any actions it took
evidence: The AI tool's permissions and which actions need human approval
Detection results for known attacks after each model update
audit_focus.recommend: Report any AI weakness that exposes data or takes unapproved actions to the application owner and security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The application owner decides on fixes and accepts any remaining risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat an AI component as a control that can be fooled. Test it with authorization, limit what it can do, keep a person able to override it, and retest after model or data changes.

exam_traps.trap: AI security tools learn on their own, so they do not need testing.
exam_traps.why: Models can be evaded, poisoned or misled, and they change with updates.

exam_traps.trap: If the assistant's instructions say 'never reveal secrets', prompt injection is not a risk.
exam_traps.why: Injected instructions can get around built-in rules. Real protection comes from limiting the AI's access and checking its actions.

key_terms.definition: A rule or filter around an AI model that limits what it accepts, says or does.
A change to an AI model or its training data; earlier test results may no longer hold.

key_terminologies.Data classification: Assigning data a sensitivity level, set by its owner, that decides how it must be protected.
key_terminologies.Labeling: Marking data with its classification so people and tools can apply the right handling rules.
key_terminologies.Data masking: Hiding real values behind fake or partial ones, for example in test data or on screens.
key_terminologies.Tokenization: Replacing a sensitive value with a random token that only a protected vault can map back.
key_terminologies.Media sanitization: Making data on media infeasible to recover by the clear, purge or destroy method.
key_terminologies.Symmetric encryption: Encryption with one shared secret key; fast, so it is used for bulk data. Needs n(n−1)/2 keys for n people.
key_terminologies.Asymmetric encryption: Encryption with a public and private key pair; used for key exchange and signatures. Needs 2n keys for n people.
key_terminologies.Hashing: A one-way function producing a fixed-length digest. A plain hash uses no key; a keyed hash (HMAC) adds one. It is not encryption.
key_terminologies.Digital signature: Proof of origin and integrity, made with the signer's private key and checked with their public key.
key_terminologies.Certificate authority (CA): A trusted organization that verifies an owner's identity and signs the certificate linking them to a public key.
key_terminologies.Post-quantum cryptography: Public-key algorithms designed to resist future quantum computers, such as the standards NIST published in 2024.
key_terminologies.Event vs incident: An event is anything observable; an incident actually or imminently harms security or violates policy, and starts the response plan.
key_terminologies.SIEM: Security information and event management: a system that collects and correlates logs and raises alerts.
key_terminologies.Security operations center (SOC): The team that monitors and responds to security events; not a System and Organization Controls (SOC) report.
key_terminologies.Alert fatigue: Missed threats caused by analysts facing more alerts than they can properly review.
key_terminologies.Malware: Malicious software, such as viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware, spyware and rootkits.
key_terminologies.Threat actor: A person or group that could cause harm, such as criminals, nation-states, hacktivists or insiders.
key_terminologies.Cyber threat intelligence (CTI): Analyzed information about threats, used to anticipate, detect and respond to attacks.
key_terminologies.MITRE ATT&CK: A free knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques, used to map detections and plan tests.
key_terminologies.Incident response plan: The approved document that sets incident definitions, roles, authority, communication and response steps.
key_terminologies.Containment: Stopping an incident from spreading, for example by isolating a host; it comes before eradication.
key_terminologies.Chain of custody: A record of everyone who handled evidence, when and why, showing it was not altered.
key_terminologies.Tabletop exercise: A discussion-based walk-through of an incident scenario to test roles and decisions, without touching systems.
key_terminologies.Asset inventory: An up-to-date list of hardware, software, data, cloud and AI assets, each with a named owner.
key_terminologies.End-of-life (EOL): A product its vendor no longer supports, so newly found flaws are not patched.
key_terminologies.Secure baseline: The approved minimum secure configuration for one type of system.
key_terminologies.Change management: The process for requesting, approving, testing, making and reviewing changes to systems.
key_terminologies.Penetration test: An authorized attempt to exploit weaknesses to show what an attacker could achieve; a scan alone is not one.
key_terminologies.SAST and DAST: Static testing examines code without running it; dynamic testing probes the running application.
key_terminologies.Prompt injection: Hidden instructions in input or content that try to make an AI tool ignore its rules.
